title: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving
tagline: Think clearly, decide well and solve real problems, with practice in every module
summary: Learn to evaluate claims and arguments, spot fallacies and biases, make structured decisions and solve problems by finding root causes. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Thinking foundations
modules.summary: What critical thinking is, how to separate fact from opinion and how to spot assumptions.
modules.outcome: You can describe the elements of critical thinking, tell facts from opinions and assumptions and ask better questions.
modules.intro: Critical thinking is not about criticising. It is the habit of asking whether something is true, whether it makes sense and what else might be going on, before you decide to believe or act. It is one of the most valued skills in study and work.

topics.title: What critical thinking is
topics.html:
Definition

Critical thinking. Careful, fair thinking that examines claims, evidence and reasoning before reaching a conclusion, and that stays open to changing that conclusion when better evidence appears.

Habits of a critical thinker
HabitIn practice
CuriousAsks questions instead of accepting at once
FairConsiders other views seriously
Evidence-ledWants to see support for claims
HumbleAdmits uncertainty and changes their mind
ClearDefines terms and states conclusions plainly

Critical thinking is not cynicism. A cynic rejects everything; a critical thinker weighs things. It is also not only logic: it includes noticing your own feelings and biases, because they shape what you accept.

Tip

When you meet a strong claim, ask yourself: 'What would I need to see to change my mind?'

Consider a simple case. A friend tells you that a new energy drink improves exam marks. A reflexive reaction is either to believe it because your friend is honest, or to scoff because it sounds too good. A critical thinker asks a few quiet questions instead. How was this measured? Compared with whom? Did students who chose the drink also happen to be those who studied longer? Who sells the drink? None of these questions accuses anyone. They simply decide how much weight the claim deserves, and they often lead to the more interesting discovery that the evidence is thinner than the confidence.

It also helps to notice that thinking is shaped by feelings. When a claim flatters us or fits what our group believes, we scrutinise it less. When it threatens us, we scrutinise it more. Critical thinkers try to apply the same standard to claims they like and claims they dislike. A practical test is to imagine the identical evidence supporting the opposite conclusion: would you accept it as readily? If not, your reaction is telling you about your preferences rather than about the evidence.

Check what you just learned

1. Critical thinking means:
  • Rejecting everything
  • Agreeing with the majority
  • Winning arguments
  • Weighing claims and evidence fairly (correct)

It is about fairness and evidence.
keyPoints: Critical thinking is fair, evidence-led and humble.
It is not cynicism.

topics.title: Fact, opinion and assumption
topics.html:
Three kinds of statement
KindTestExample
FactCan be checked against evidenceThe library has 12,000 books (check the records)
OpinionA judgement or preferenceThe library is the best place to study
AssumptionTaken for granted without checkingEveryone knows where the library is

Opinions are not bad. Good opinions are supported by facts and reasons. The skill is knowing which one you are looking at, especially when a statement mixes them.

Worked example

Untangling a sentence

'The new bus route is a failure because nobody uses it.'

  1. Opinion: it is a failure.
  2. Possible fact: the number of riders is low (check the figures).
  3. Assumption: 'nobody' means few; low use means failure.

Answer. Break statements into parts and test each.

Common mistakes

  • Treating a confident tone as proof.
  • Treating a fact as an opinion because you dislike it.
  • Not noticing your own assumptions.

Check what you just learned

1. 'Everyone will like it' is most likely:
  • An assumption (correct)
  • A fact
  • A measurement
  • A proof

It is taken for granted.
keyPoints: Check facts, support opinions and expose assumptions.
Break mixed statements into parts.

topics.title: Asking good questions
topics.html:
Questions that test a claim

  • What exactly is being claimed?
  • What is the evidence, and where does it come from?
  • Is the source reliable and unbiased?
  • What is missing from the picture?
  • What are other explanations?
  • Who gains if I believe this?
Source check
QuestionWhy
Who wrote it?Expertise and motive
When was it published?Is it out of date?
How do they know?Data, interviews or opinion?
Do other independent sources agree?Reduces the risk of a single error
Watch out

Social media and messages can spread false information fast. Before you share, check at least one reliable source.

Check what you just learned

1. Before sharing a surprising claim you should:
  • Share first
  • Check a reliable source (correct)
  • Ignore it
  • Add emojis

Verify first.

Key terms: flip and sort

Claim
A statement to be supported
Evidence
Information that supports a claim
Assumption
Something taken for granted
Bias
A tendency that distorts judgement
keyPoints: Ask what, how do they know and what else could explain it.
Check sources before sharing.

modules.title: Arguments and evidence
modules.summary: Break arguments into parts, judge evidence and spot common fallacies.
modules.outcome: You can map an argument, judge the strength of evidence and name common fallacies.
modules.intro: An argument is a claim supported by reasons. Whether you are reading an article, writing an essay or discussing a plan, you need to see its parts and judge how well they fit.

topics.title: The parts of an argument
topics.html:
Example
PartContent
ClaimThe library should open until 10 pm
Reason 1Students need quiet study space in the evening
Evidence 162% of 200 surveyed students cannot study well in hostels
AssumptionStaff and cost can be managed
ObjectionExtra hours cost too much
ReplyShift existing hours; cost about 40,000 a month

An argument is strong when the reasons are true, they really support the claim, and the writer has dealt with the best objections. It is weak when any of those fail.

Tip

To map an argument, ask: what is the conclusion, why should I believe it, and what would have to be true for the reasons to work?

Check what you just learned

1. An assumption in an argument is:
  • Always stated
  • A conclusion
  • Often unstated (correct)
  • Proof

It must be exposed.
keyPoints: Claim, reasons, evidence, assumptions and objections.
Strong arguments have true reasons that support the claim.

topics.title: Judging evidence
topics.html:
Kinds of evidence and cautions
KindStrengthCaution
Statistics and dataCan be strong and checkableSample size, who was asked, how it was measured
Expert opinionUseful when the expert is relevant and independentExperts can disagree or have interests
Personal storyVivid and relatableMay not be typical
AnalogyHelps explainRarely proves
Authority or popularityWeak aloneTruth is not decided by numbers or titles

Questions about data

  • How many were included, and how were they chosen?
  • Compared with what?
  • Is the measure what it claims to be?
  • Is the source independent?
  • Does the data show cause or only connection?
Watch out

Correlation is not causation. Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer, but one does not cause the other. Look for a third factor: hot weather.

Worked example

Weak versus strong

'My uncle never wore a seat belt and lived to 90.' versus 'In a study of 50,000 crashes, belted drivers were far less likely to die.'

  1. The first is one story.
  2. The second is large-scale data.
  3. Prefer the evidence that is broad and checkable.

Answer. One story cannot overturn a pattern in thousands of cases.

Check what you just learned

1. Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer because:
  • Ice cream causes drowning
  • It is random
  • Drowning causes ice-cream sales
  • A third factor, heat, affects both (correct)

Look for a hidden cause.
keyPoints: Judge data by sample, source and comparison.
Correlation is not causation.

topics.title: Common fallacies
topics.html:
Fallacies to know
NameWhat it doesExample
Attack on the personAttacks the speaker instead of the ideaYou cannot trust her idea, she failed maths
Straw manDistorts the other view then attacks itHe wants shorter exams, so he wants us to learn nothing
Slippery slopeClaims one step leads to disaster without proofOne late submission will end all discipline
False choiceOffers only two options when more existRaise prices or close the shop
Appeal to popularityEveryone does it, so it is rightMillions use it, so it is safe
Circular reasoningUses the conclusion as a reasonIt is true because it says so

Fallacies are persuasive because they borrow the shape of good reasoning. 'Millions of people use it' resembles evidence of quality; an attack on someone's character resembles a reason to doubt their claim. The remedy is to ask what the statement actually shows. Does the number of users say anything about safety? Does a person's past mistake say anything about today's budget figures? Often the honest answer is: very little. Learning to ask this question calmly, without scorn, makes you both a better listener and a harder person to mislead.

Pointing out a fallacy is not the same as proving the conclusion false. A conclusion can be true even if the argument for it is poor. The point is that the argument does not support it.

Common mistakes

  • Calling every disagreement a fallacy.
  • Using fallacy names to dismiss people.
  • Committing the same fallacies yourself when you are emotional.

Check what you just learned

1. Saying 'Everyone does it' is:
  • Appeal to popularity (correct)
  • A straw man
  • Circular
  • Proof

Popularity is not truth.

Key terms: flip and sort

Premise
A reason offered for a conclusion
Fallacy
A flaw in reasoning
Correlation
Two things changing together
Causation
One thing causing another
keyPoints: Name the common fallacies and explain what is wrong.
A bad argument does not make the conclusion false.

options: Uses the conclusion as the reason
The argument is weak, not necessarily the conclusion false

modules.title: Decisions and judgement
modules.summary: Make better decisions: weigh options, avoid common biases and live with uncertainty.
modules.outcome: You can compare options with weighted criteria, recognise common biases and make a decision memo.
modules.intro: Decisions shape results more than almost any other skill. Good decisions come from a good process, not just good luck; a good process does not guarantee a good outcome, but it improves your odds over time.

topics.title: A simple decision process
topics.html:
Writing the options and criteria down stops you from jumping to the first idea, and it exposes what you really care about. A decision made in your head is hard to improve.

How weights change the winner

Change the weight on price and see how the weighted scores change for two options.

Adjust Weight on price (percent), Option A price score (1-10), Option A quality score (1-10), Option B price score (1-10), Option B quality score (1-10) and see Option A weighted score, Option B weighted score change.

Tip

If two options score almost the same, the decision does not matter much. Pick one and move on.

Check what you just learned

1. Why list at least three options?
  • It is a rule
  • It avoids a false choice (correct)
  • It takes time
  • It looks formal

Two options are often a false choice.
keyPoints: Define, list options, weight criteria, score and review.
Writing it down exposes what you care about.

topics.title: Biases that bend judgement
topics.html:
Common biases
BiasWhat happensCounter
Confirmation biasWe seek evidence that agrees with usLook for the best case against your view
AnchoringThe first number or idea shapes later judgementForm your own estimate first; compare many sources
Sunk costWe continue because of past spendingAsk: if I were starting today, would I choose this?
AvailabilityVivid examples feel commonUse statistics rather than memorable stories
OverconfidenceWe think we know more than we doState a range and check outcomes over time
GroupthinkPeople go along with the groupAsk for dissent and write opinions privately first
Worked example

Sunk cost

A student has studied a course for two years but is unhappy and the job market for it is poor.

  1. Past effort cannot be recovered whatever she chooses.
  2. The relevant question is which future path is best.
  3. Continuing only to avoid 'wasting' the past may waste more.

Answer. Decide on future costs and benefits only.

Common mistakes

  • Believing you are free of bias.
  • Using bias names to dismiss people.
  • Making major decisions when tired, hungry or angry.

Check what you just learned

1. Sunk cost thinking says:
  • Never stop
  • Always continue
  • Past spending should not drive future choices (correct)
  • Ignore the future

Only the future matters.
keyPoints: Everyone has biases; build counters into your process.
Ignore sunk costs.

topics.title: Uncertainty and risk
topics.html:
Most decisions are made without full knowledge. Thinking in probabilities and ranges, not certainties, leads to better choices and less regret.

Formula · Expected value

expected value = (chance of gain × gain) − (chance of loss × loss)

A 30% chance of winning 100,000 and a 70% chance of losing 20,000 has expected value 0.3×100,000 − 0.7×20,000 = 16,000.

Practical habits

  • Ask 'What is the worst case, and can I live with it?'
  • Give a number to your confidence: 'I am about 70% sure'.
  • Look for options that are cheap to reverse.
  • Run a small test before a big commitment.
  • Review decisions after the outcome to learn from the process, not just the result.
Watch out

Do not judge a decision only by its result. A good decision can have a bad outcome by chance, and a poor decision can get lucky.

Check what you just learned

1. A reversible decision should be:
  • Treated like an irreversible one
  • Never reviewed
  • Avoided
  • Made faster with less worry (correct)

Cheap to undo means lower stakes.

Key terms: flip and sort

Criteria
The factors used to judge options
Weight
How much a criterion matters
Bias
A systematic error in judgement
Sunk cost
Money or effort already spent
Expected value
Probability-weighted outcome
keyPoints: Think in probabilities and ranges.
Judge decisions by process as well as outcome.

modules.title: Problem solving
modules.summary: Define problems precisely, find root causes and generate and test solutions.
modules.outcome: You can write a clear problem statement, find root causes with five whys and Pareto analysis and choose and test a solution.
modules.intro: A well-defined problem is half solved. Many failed solutions come from solving the wrong problem or treating a symptom.

topics.title: Define the problem
topics.html:
A good problem statement

  1. Describes what is wrong, with a number.
  2. Says where and when it happens.
  3. Says who is affected.
  4. Does not hide a solution or blame.
Vague and clear
VagueClear
Sales are badWeekend sales have fallen 20% in two months while weekdays are steady
Customers are unhappy27% of orders last week arrived late, causing 40 complaints
The team is slowReports take six days instead of three

Before solving, ask: what would 'solved' look like? A target such as 'weekend sales back within 5% of the old level in four weeks' gives you a way to know.

Tip

Write the problem in one sentence and show it to someone else. If they ask 'What do you mean?', it is not yet clear.

Check what you just learned

1. A good problem statement:
  • Includes a number and context (correct)
  • Is vague
  • Contains a solution
  • Blames someone

Precision helps.
keyPoints: State the problem with numbers, place and time.
Define what 'solved' means.

topics.title: Find root causes
topics.html:
Worked example

Five whys in action

Problem: half of checkout customers left.

  1. 1. Many saw an error at payment.
  2. 2. The card form failed.
  3. 3. An update changed how the field was sent.
  4. 4. It was not tested on mobile.
  5. 5. The release process has no mobile test.
  6. Root cause: no mobile test step.

Answer. Fixing the form fixes this week; fixing the process fixes the future.

Pareto analysis
IdeaUse
A few causes create most of the problemCount causes and rank them
Cumulative shareFind the few that make up about 80%
Act on the vital fewFocus where effort pays most
Watch out

Stopping at the first 'because' is the commonest mistake. The first answer is usually a symptom.

Be careful that the five whys does not turn into a hunt for someone to blame. If the chain ends with 'because Ravi forgot', the process has probably stopped too early. Ask why it was possible to forget, why nothing caught the mistake and why the system depended on one person's memory. Good root causes usually point to a missing check, an unclear rule or a missing tool, all of which can be fixed, rather than to a person's character, which cannot.

Check what you just learned

1. Pareto analysis helps by:
  • Listing all causes equally
  • Finding the few causes behind most of the problem (correct)
  • Choosing a colour
  • Removing data

Focus on the biggest.
keyPoints: Use five whys to go beyond the first cause.
Use Pareto analysis to find the vital few.

topics.title: Generate and test solutions
topics.html:
Generate

  • Brainstorm many ideas before judging any.
  • Combine and improve ideas.
  • Ask 'What would make this problem disappear?'.
  • Look at how others solved similar problems.
Choose with criteria
CriterionQuestion
ImpactHow much of the problem will it solve?
CostWhat will it cost in money and time?
SpeedHow fast can we start?
RiskWhat could go wrong, and can we undo it?

Common mistakes

  • Jumping to the first idea.
  • Running a big change without a pilot.
  • Declaring victory without measuring.

Check what you just learned

1. Before a big rollout you should:
  • Wait a year
  • Skip testing
  • Pilot it (correct)
  • Announce success

Test small first.

Key terms: flip and sort

Problem statement
A clear description of what is wrong
Root cause
The underlying reason
Five whys
Asking why repeatedly
Pareto
A few causes cause most effects
Pilot
A small test
keyPoints: Brainstorm, choose by criteria, pilot and measure.
Monitor after rollout.

modules.title: Creative and systems thinking
modules.summary: Generate new ideas and see how parts of a system affect each other.
modules.outcome: You can use simple creative techniques and describe feedback loops and side effects in a system.
modules.intro: Analysis finds what is wrong; creativity finds what could be. Systems thinking reminds us that actions have side effects that ripple through connected parts.

topics.title: Creative techniques
topics.html:
Techniques
TechniqueHow it worksExample
BrainstormingGenerate many ideas without judgingTwenty ways to reduce waste in the canteen
Reverse thinkingAsk how to make the problem worse, then flipHow to make students dislike the library? Then do the opposite
AnalogyBorrow a solution from another fieldQueue design in airports for hospital waiting
ConstraintsImpose a limit to force inventionA solution costing under 1,000 rupees
SCAMPERSubstitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, reverseApply each to a product

Creativity is a habit, not a gift. People who produce good ideas produce many ideas, including bad ones, and then select.

Tip

Separate generating from judging. Give ideas a time to exist before you evaluate them.

Check what you just learned

1. During brainstorming you should:
  • Judge every idea
  • Stay silent
  • Keep only one
  • Generate many ideas first (correct)

Quantity then quality.
keyPoints: Use techniques to generate many ideas, then select.
Separate idea generation from judging.

topics.title: Thinking in systems
topics.html:
Definition

System. A set of connected parts that together produce results, where changing one part affects others.

Feedback loops
TypeEffectExample
ReinforcingAmplifies changeMore users attract more users; panic selling causes more selling
BalancingResists change and stabilisesA thermostat; hunger leading to eating
Worked example

Side effects

A college bans cars to reduce traffic.

  1. More students ride scooters, raising accidents.
  2. Shops nearby lose customers and complain.
  3. Lesson: ask who else is affected and what changes elsewhere.

Answer. Good solutions think a step or two ahead.

Questions

  • What are the parts and how are they connected?
  • What loops reinforce or balance?
  • Where are the delays?
  • What could this change cause somewhere else?

Check what you just learned

1. A reinforcing loop:
  • Amplifies change (correct)
  • Stabilises change
  • Does nothing
  • Stops systems

It grows what is happening.
keyPoints: Look for connections, loops, delays and side effects.
Ask what else will change.

topics.title: Working with others on problems
topics.html:
Hard problems are often solved by groups. But groups can fall into groupthink or be dominated by loud voices. A few simple practices keep thinking fair.

Practices

  • Write ideas silently before discussing.
  • Invite people who disagree to speak first.
  • Assign someone to argue the opposite case.
  • Record decisions and reasons.
  • Review the outcome later.
Roles in a thinking session
RoleJob
FacilitatorKeeps time and invites everyone
ScribeRecords ideas and decisions
ChallengerQuestions assumptions
SponsorDecides what will be done
Watch out

Hierarchy can silence honest views. Leaders should speak last.

Check what you just learned

1. To reduce groupthink you can:
  • Discourage questions
  • Ask for dissent (correct)
  • Vote publicly first
  • Follow the leader

Invite challenge.

Key terms: flip and sort

SCAMPER
A checklist for creative change
System
Connected parts producing results
Feedback loop
An effect that returns to affect its cause
Facilitator
A person guiding the discussion
keyPoints: Write first, discuss second; invite dissent.
Leaders speak last.

modules.title: Thinking in practice
modules.summary: Apply the tools to study, work and everyday information, and keep improving.
modules.outcome: You can evaluate news and claims, write a short reasoned recommendation and build a habit of reflection.
modules.intro: Skills become habits through use. This final module applies critical thinking to everyday information, writing and work.

topics.title: Evaluating news and online claims
topics.html:
Warning signs
SignMeaning
Strong emotion, urgent toneDesigned to spread before you think
No source or dateCannot be checked
Too good or too awful to be trueCheck twice
Screenshot without a linkMay be edited
Only one outletLook for independent confirmation

Useful habits

  • Read beyond the headline.
  • Search for the claim with the word 'fact check'.
  • Check the date and location of photos.
  • Be willing to say 'I do not know yet'.
Watch out

Be careful with health, money and safety claims: acting on false information can cost a lot. Use official or professional sources.

Check what you just learned

1. A warning sign of misleading content is:
  • A named source and a date
  • A link to evidence
  • An urgent, emotional tone and no source (correct)
  • A correction notice

It is designed to spread.
keyPoints: Stop, check the source, find evidence and confirm independently.
Be careful with emotionally charged content.

topics.title: Writing a reasoned recommendation
topics.html:
Structure
SectionContent
ProblemWhat needs deciding
Possible causes or optionsSeveral, not one
EvidenceWhat you know and what you need
Options with pros and consA fair comparison
Recommendation and testA choice, a pilot and a measure
Worked example

A short recommendation

Weekend bakery sales have dropped 20%.

  1. Check stock-out times first.
  2. If stock runs out before noon, increase baking by 15% and message regular customers.
  3. Measure: weekend sales back within 5% in four weeks.

Answer. A recommendation includes a test and a measure of success.

Tip

Write for a reader who is smart but busy: one clear recommendation, three reasons, one risk.

Check what you just learned

1. A strong recommendation includes:
  • No options
  • A hidden agenda
  • Only opinion
  • A measure of success (correct)

Otherwise you cannot learn.
keyPoints: Present problem, evidence, options and a tested recommendation.
Include a measure of success.

topics.title: Reflection and growth
topics.html:
The best thinkers review their own thinking. After an important decision or problem, take five minutes to write what happened and what you learned.

A reflection routine

  • What did I decide, and why?
  • What did I expect, and what happened?
  • What did I miss?
  • What bias might have affected me?
  • What will I do differently next time?
Habits to keep
HabitFrequency
Read widely, including views you disagree withWeekly
Check one claim you sawDaily
Write a short decision journalAfter major decisions
Ask for feedback on your reasoningMonthly
Tip

Admitting 'I was wrong' is a strength. It is how thinking improves.

Check what you just learned

1. A decision journal helps you:
  • Learn from your reasoning (correct)
  • Hide mistakes
  • Avoid deciding
  • Impress others

It builds judgement over time.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fact check
Verification of a claim
Independent source
A source unconnected with the first
Decision journal
A record of reasoning
Reflection
Looking back to learn
keyPoints: Reflect after decisions; keep a decision journal.
Be willing to say 'I was wrong'.
